title: SYSK Selects: How Shrunken Heads Work
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of the episode "Shrunken Heads," originally run June 2011. Josh introduces it as one of the show's all-time great episodes. The hosts discuss why cannibalism is hard to document compared with head shrinking, which is tied to the Shuar (Jívaro) people of the Ecuadorian and Peruvian Amazon. They cover the revenge logic behind head-taking (spirits, bewitchment, the tsantsa), the raid and the step-by-step shrinking process (skinning, boiling, sewing shut, hot-stone drying, charcoal rubbing), the year-long celebrations (feasts with chicha), the trade of shrunken heads with Europeans and the resulting increase in killing, counterfeits (sloth, monkey, goat, and stolen human heads), museum repatriation debates, and a 1996 rumor about Ecuadorian soldiers during the Cenepa War. The episode closes with listener mail thank-yous.

segments.title: Selects intro and opening banter
segments.summary: Josh introduces this Selects episode as a rerun of Shrunken Heads from June 2011. The hosts joke about WFMU airing the show and compare head shrinking with cannibalism as gruesome practices.

segments.title: Shuar head shrinking and Spanish colonial rule
segments.summary: The hosts explain that the Shuar (Jivaro) are the best-documented head shrinkers, that the term Jivaro is a derogatory name, and that the Shuar repelled Spanish colonial rule in an uprising that killed many colonists. The Nazi-era claims about shrunken heads are mentioned as unverified.

segments.title: Revenge, spirits and the raid
segments.summary: The hosts describe the belief that unseen deaths were caused by bewitchment, which required retribution. Ayahuasca-type hallucinogens (described as a jungle vine) were used to consult spirits. Raiders gave warning, sometimes spared children's heads, and then killed with spears.

segments.title: Taking the head and the ritual process
segments.summary: The raiders cut the head with a V-shaped incision, tie the head up, and flee, abandoning weapons. The tsantsa-making process is led by an elder called the kuraka. Heads carry three meanings: proof of revenge, a spiritual vessel, and social status.

segments.title: Step-by-step shrinking process
segments.summary: The skin is removed from the skull with the eyes and cartilage discarded. The skin is boiled for about thirty minutes, dried, and the lips and orifices are sewn shut. Hot stones, pebbles and sand are used to shrink the head, which is then smoothed and blackened with charcoal ash and dried over a fire.

segments.title: Year-long feasts, chicha, and the head trade
segments.summary: The head is worn for a year, with feasts including chicha beer and ceremonial dancing. The heads later lost significance and were given away or sold. Europeans traded guns for heads, which increased warfare and population decline.

segments.title: Counterfeits, museums and repatriation
segments.summary: Sloth, monkey, goat and horse-skin heads were made as forgeries, and stolen human heads from Ecuadorian morgues were used. Authentic tsantsas have sewn lips and cords. Museums are reconsidering their collections, and a DNA test on a shrunken head was reported.

segments.title: Christian missionaries and modern rumors
segments.summary: Christian missionaries reduced head taking. The hosts mention a 1996 rumor that Ecuadorian soldiers made shrunken heads of Peruvian soldiers during the Cenepa War, which has been largely dismissed.

segments.title: Listener mail and thank-yous
segments.summary: The hosts thank listeners for gifts and postcards, including Archie comics, germ plushies, chocolate, beef jerky, and a personal dentist referral. They invite listeners to write to the show's email address.
